nameStory: Red columbine gets its name from the Latin 'columba' meaning dove, because the flower's five spurs were thought to look like five doves drinking together around a dish. The red refers to the distinctive bright red and yellow coloration that makes this wildflower so eye-catching in the spring woods.
description: Red columbine is a delicate woodland wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall with an airy, graceful appearance. Its most striking feature is the drooping, bell-shaped flowers with distinctive red petals and yellow centers, each flower sporting five hollow spurs that curve backward like tiny horns. The blue-green leaves are deeply divided into three rounded leaflets that have a soft, almost rubbery texture. This native perennial creates lovely clumps in shaded gardens and wild areas throughout New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Drooping, bell-shaped flowers with bright red outer petals and yellow inner petals, plus five distinctive hollow spurs that curve backward like tiny elephant trunks - no other New England wildflower has this unique combination

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Blue-green leaves divided into three rounded, fan-shaped leaflets with scalloped edges that feel slightly thick and rubbery to the touch, growing on long, slender stalks

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows 1-3 feet tall with a loose, airy appearance and branching stems that seem to dance in the breeze, often forming small colonies

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops into clusters of pointed, papery seed pods that split open to release small black seeds with a slight shine

habitat: Look for red columbine on rocky slopes, woodland edges, and partially shaded areas with well-drained soil throughout New England's forests. It thrives in the dappled sunlight of deciduous woods and is often found growing from cracks in rocky outcrops or stone walls. This adaptable native also does well in woodland gardens and naturalized areas with similar conditions.

seasonality.spring: Flowers bloom from late April through June, creating the most spectacular display when the drooping red and yellow bells are at their peak.
seasonality.summer: After flowering, the distinctive three-part leaves remain attractive through summer, and seed pods begin to develop and mature.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods split open to release seeds, and the foliage may turn yellow before dying back to the ground for winter.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to the ground, leaving no above-ground parts visible until spring growth emerges.

funFact: Red columbine flowers are perfectly designed for ruby-throated hummingbirds - the red color attracts them, while the long spurs match the exact length of a hummingbird's beak and tongue, making this one of the few native New England flowers specifically evolved for hummingbird pollination.
confusionNotes: The distinctive spurred flowers make red columbine nearly impossible to confuse with any other New England wildflower when in bloom. The three-part leaves might remind you of wild ginger, but ginger has much larger, heart-shaped leaves and completely different flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Canadian columbine,' this species is actually native throughout eastern North America, not just Canada. The scientific name 'canadensis' simply means 'from Canada' and was applied by early botanists who first described specimens from that region.
compareHints: Red columbine is the only native columbine species in New England, making it easy to distinguish from the escaped garden columbines you might occasionally find. Garden columbines typically have larger, more upright flowers in blue, purple, white, or mixed colors, while our native red columbine always has the characteristic drooping red and yellow flowers with more delicate proportions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common columbine can be distinguished from our native red columbine by its blue or purple flowers (versus bright red and yellow) and its more robust, bushier growth habit.
Blue columbine stands out from its eastern cousin, red columbine, primarily by color - blue and white versus red and yellow.
Dark columbine is easily separated from our native red columbine by its dark purple-black flowers versus red and yellow ones.
Golden columbine stands out from other columbines by its pure yellow flowers and extra-long spurs.
